NEW DELHI: OVHcloud launched 55 new products across its cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) portfolio at the OVHcloud AI Summit. The expanded offerings cover infrastructure to applications, including orchestration, inference, and AI-augmented Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) services.The company is integrating NVIDIA RTX 6000 Pro, Blackwell B300, and Rubin R200 GPUs into its Bare Metal and Public Cloud services. Its data centres can supply up to 60,000 B300 GPUs or 35,000 R200 GPUs.New Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)-based network services include a Web Application Firewall (WAF), a Virtual Private Network (VPN), VPC peering, VPC endpoints, an Application Load Balancer (ALB), a Global Load Balancer, and private DNS. Customers can manage public IP address announcement and routing with BGP Service, and use their own IP ranges with BYOIP. OVHcloud Connect is now available at 40 points of presence globally.For AI inference, AI Fabric, built with Blade.sh, enables Python agent sandbox launches. Public Cloud also offers Serverless Containers, Serverless Functions, and Messaging & Events. AI Endpoints has added approximately 100 new models, including voice and image, along with governance tools. Gladia extends the offering to real-time and recorded speech transcription and voice generation in over 100 languages.AI Agents hosts, scales, secures, and monitors agents connected to enterprise tools via nearly 480 connectors and MCP servers. AI Search allows businesses to explore documents using semantic and lexical search across millions of documents per collection.Application security features include Anti-DDoS Customer Profiles for tailored protection, Cloud Hardware Security Module (HSM) for encryption key management, and Confidential Computing for data encryption during processing. Backup Center, Certificate Manager, and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) complete the security suite.Yaniv Fdida, chief product and technology officer (CPTO) of OVHcloud, said that moving AI projects into production often involves juggling multiple products and providers. He said OVHcloud offers an integrated user experience with an open, reversible, and predictable European offering through a single provider.

stories.title: From E-Commerce to Silicon: How Selangor Built Its Semiconductor Chapter
stories.summary: From SITEC in 2015 to two IC design parks, a chip fund and a talent academy, this is how Sidec is putting Selangor on the semiconductor map.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 从电子商务到Silicon：Selangor如何构建其半导体篇章
stories.content:
Selangor is no longer just following the global semiconductor story. It's writing a chapter of it.

In 2015, when Selangor made a deliberate move and set up SITEC, the Selangor Information Technology & E-Commerce Council, to put the state’s SMEs and entrepreneurs at the forefront of the digital economy. A year later came Top ECM, Malaysia’s first e-commerce awards, built on the same conviction: digital commerce wasn’t a niche, it was the future, and Selangor meant to lead it.

By 2021, the ambition had outgrown the name. SITEC became the Selangor Information Technology & Digital Economy Corporation (Sidec), with a mandate that now covers startups, deep tech, AI, smart cities and semiconductors. That last area opened a new chapter in 2024, when Sidec led the setting up of the Malaysia Semiconductor IC Design Park in Puchong. IC Design Park 2 followed in Cyberjaya in November 2025, adding labs for validation, testing and verification.

This wasn't just about growing bigger. It signalled that Selangor would compete at every layer of the digital economy, not only the one it started in.

This year, Sidec introduces the Selangor Triple Accelerator Programme, bringing its accelerator work together under three tracks: deep tech, retail and digital assets. It builds on the Selangor Accelerator Programme, which Sidec started in 2018. Across 14 cohorts, the programme has drawn 2,251 applications and supported 470 companies, which have gone on to raise RM216 million.

Every company reaches a point where it needs a hand, and each track meets a different need. Deep-X backs founders working in AI, robotics and semiconductor-adjacent technologies, helping them advance their technologies to investment readiness. Retail-X helps SMEs and retail brands adopt AI-driven commerce and digital tools. Token-X gives founders building in digital assets the grounding they need to work with blockchain-based finance.

### Building Selangor’s Next Generation

The accelerator is one part of a wider effort. Every company hits a point where it needs a hand, and since 2015, Sidec has run more than 100 initiatives for founders ready to scale and SMEs ready to go digital and adopt AI. Together, they have empowered more than 80,000 techpreneurs and generated RM865.1 million in GMV.

### Beyond the programme

Some of the companies that came through Sidec's programmes and kept going:

- **Simplify.my | Selangor Deep Tech Xccelerator 2025** The legal-tech platform has processed more than 25,000 transactions since 2023 and works with over 260 partner law firms. It's backed by RM150,000 in pre-seed funding from 1337 Ventures. Southeast Asia is next.
- **Xtractify | Selangor Accelerator Programme 2024** The company says it reached millions in annual recurring revenue within 18 months. Its ENNO platform helps enterprises manage LLM costs, data privacy and compliance. It's now expanding regionally and targeting eight-digit ARR by 2028.
- **The Pastels Shop | Selangor E-Commerce Xccelerator 2023** The brand is now in nearly 1,000 outlets across Malaysia, including Guardian, AEON, Giant and MR.DIY. It also has an official presence in Brunei and Singapore.
- **Swipey| Selangor Accelerator Programme 2022** The platform serves more than 2,000 companies, including Maxis and MyDIGITAL. Its work with Malaysia Debt Ventures Bhd has helped make grant disbursements more transparent for SMEs.
- **Ejen2u| Selangor Accelerator Programme 2020** The company raised RM7 million from Gobi Partners, Artem Ventures, Hive SEA and Cradle Ventures. Its Ejengo platform has passed RM1 billion in transactions. Its community platform, Komuniti.io, generated around RM1.4 million for 180 communities within 10 months of launch.
- **Borong | Selangor Accelerator Programme 2018** Borong, formerly Dropee, topped the Financial Times' High-Growth Companies Asia-Pacific 2026 ranking, up from second place the year before. The company reports growing from USD300,000 in revenue to over USD99 million since it was founded in 2017.

### Malaysia Semiconductor IC Design Park

The Malaysia Semiconductor IC Design Park was years in the making. Sidec spent three to four years talking with industry partners about what an IC design park would need, and by January 2024, the partners were ready. Seven months later, IC Design Park 1 opened its doors in Puchong.

The IC Design Park is one of three pillars. It provides the infrastructure, a base for chip design and innovation. Capital comes through the Ehsan Semiconductor Fund, which is targeting RM100 million. Talent is developed through ASEM, which trains engineers in AI and semiconductor skills.

IC Design Park 1 gives companies shared access to EDA design tools, testing equipment, servers and wafer runs. It’s home to 20 companies, with SkyeChip, Oppstar and GreatAsic anchoring the local side alongside players from China, Taiwan, France, Japan and Australia.

IC Design Park 2 in Cyberjaya, launched by the Prime Minister in November 2025, takes the ecosystem from design into testing and validation. It houses what is billed as Southeast Asia’s first Advanced Chip Testing Centre, and is also home to ASEM, Sidec’s talent development arm.

### Malaysia’s homegrown chips

“The challenge for Malaysia is that we always underestimate ourselves. We just need to showcase what we’ve built and believe in ourselves.” — Yong Kai Ping, CEO of Sidec

Companies at the IC Design Park now have locally designed products to show for their work. Six of them span edge AI, AI memory, programmable logic, drone flight control, and automotive and space power.

- MARS1000 Edge AI Processor, SkyeChip
- aiDAPTIV AI Acceleration Platform, MaiStorage
- FPGA chip, Silicon X (described by the company as Malaysia’s first)
- Alphaswift FC Mini Flight Controller, Alphaswift Industries
- Maxwell Automotive LDO, Infinecs Systems
- Conan - Space-Grade Power Protection & Management Chip, Weeroc Space

### Beyond the IC Design Park

Sidec’s work in the ecosystem extends to data centres. Under Selangor’s Local Economic Development (LED) initiative, new data centres are encouraged to source 30% of their server and machine content from local suppliers. Sidec supports operators in meeting that target by connecting them with local suppliers and providing technical expertise.

Looking further ahead, Sidec is exploring a future push into physical AI, meaning robots and drones for security patrols and port or airport logistics. It’s an early-stage ambition, not yet realised, but Sidec sees it as a natural next step for the design capability being built at the IC Design Park.

### The capital behind Selangor's chip designers

A semiconductor ecosystem is only as strong as the people who run it. ASEM, Sidec’s talent development arm, has trained around 850 engineers and works with more than 100 universities worldwide.

Selected engineers train for six weeks at no cost, paying only for their own lodging, and the top 10% go overseas for advanced training. Graduates can expect a starting salary of around RM5,000 a month, and all have been placed in on-the-job training or permanent roles. ASEM has also upskilled 50 lecturers.

Two programmes carry that ambition. The National Semiconductor Excellence Program (NSEP) turns third- and fourth-year students and back-end talent into IC design engineers. In 2025, it trained 455 engineers in digital IC design, embedded systems, robotics and AI, with training leading into job placement.

The Global Semiconductor Exchange Program (GSEP) builds a foundation locally, then sends engineers abroad for hands-on training: SoC and RISC-V processor design at IIT Madras in India, and analog IC design in Shenzhen, China. In 2026, 90 engineers trained overseas through the programme.

ASEM’s partnerships have expanded quickly. Between September 2024 and December 2025, it formed partnerships with Purdue University in Indiana, \[SZIIT or SUSTech, confirm\] in Shenzhen, the Bangladesh-Malaysia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BMCCI), the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) in Chennai, and The Institution of Engineers, Malaysia (IEM) Sarawak in Kuching.

Around 400 engineers now work across the Park's companies. Sidec wants working in Selangor to come with a life around the work.That's the idea behind Living Ecosystem: one platform for the engineers at the Park and the founders at Sidec's Startup Campus.

Every week, Sidec runs activities ranging from badminton and pickleball to hiking and running, with roughly 50 to 80 people turning up each time. The sessions are simple, and that’s the point: engineers and founders who might never otherwise meet get to know each other outside the office. Sidec is also working with Tourism Selangor on community trips, so members can see more of the state together.

A good job can bring an engineer to Selangor. A community is more likely to keep them here.

### About Sidec

Sidec (Selangor Information Technology & Digital Economy Corporation) is the Selangor state agency driving the growth of the state’s digital economy. Established in 2015, Sidec supports startups, SMEs and tech talent through programmes in entrepreneurship, digital adoption, deep tech, AI, smart cities and semiconductors. Its initiatives include the Selangor Triple Accelerator Programme, the Malaysia Semiconductor IC Design Park and AiSEM@Selangor, the state’s AI and semiconductor summit. Sidec also co-established Ehsan Kapital, the general partner of the Ehsan Semiconductor Fund, and is the parent company of the Advanced Semiconductor Academy of Malaysia (ASEM). To date, Sidec has run more than 100 initiatives, empowered more than 80,000 techpreneurs and generated RM865.1 million in GMV.

For more information, visit www.sidec.com.my.

stories.title: PDG expands Tokyo TY1 green financing to US$327 million
stories.summary: Princeton Digital Group has expanded green financing for its TY1 campus in Greater Tokyo to $327 million through additional commitments from BNP Paribas, ING, and two other banks. The increased facility supports PDG's strategy of aligning its Japan expansion with sustainability-linked financing instruments as investor scrutiny of data center carbon intensity intensifies.
stories.why_it_matters: The expanded green financing demonstrates that sustainability-linked debt instruments are becoming standard for large-scale APAC data center development, creating a bifurcation between operators who can access preferential ESG capital and those reliant on conventional financing. For Japan specifically, the structure reinforces its attractiveness to international investors seeking lower-carbon infrastructure exposure in a region where coal-dependent markets face increasing capital access challenges.

stories.why_zh: 扩大的green financing表明，可持续发展挂钩债务工具正成为大规模APAC data center开发的标准，能够在运营商之间造成分化：那些能够获取优惠ESG资本的运营商与依赖传统融资的运营商。具体对Japan而言，该结构增强了其对寻求在该区域降低碳基础设施敞口的国际投资者的吸引力，而依赖煤炭的市场正面临日益增加的资本获取挑战。
stories.content:
Princeton Digital Group (PDG), a data center operator in the Asia-Pacific region, has announced a JPY 33 billion (US$ 210 million) increase in green financing for its flagship TY1 campus in Saitama, Greater Tokyo, Japan, taking total green financing for the facility to JPY 51.5 billion (US$ 327 million).

Four banks, namely BNP Paribas, ING, OCBC, and Société Générale, provided the green financing, some of which were lenders in the original loan. PDG stated in a press release that the financing would fund the continued development of the 96 MW TY1 campus. The transaction contributes to PDG’s plan to raise up to US$ 5 billion in debt financing to deliver data center capacity across the Asia-Pacific region.

“The continued support of our existing banking partners, alongside the participation of new lenders, reflects confidence in PDG,” said Rangu Salgame, PDG Chairman, Chief Executive Officer, and Co-Founder.

The financing is structured under PDG’s Green Finance Framework, which supports the development of energy-efficient digital infrastructure. As w.media reported earlier this month, the same framework was used to secure RM 4.9 billion (US$ 1.3 billion) in financing for PDG’s JH1 campus in Johor, Malaysia.

TY1 is a two-building campus 30 km north of central Tokyo in Saitama City. The campus has achieved LEED v4 Building Design and Construction: Core and Shell Development certification. It is also the first data center in Japan to achieve OCP Ready v2 for Hyperscale and NVIDIA DGX-Ready Data Center certification for liquid cooling. PDG said the facility has attracted top hyperscalers and helped to establish Saitama as an important hyperscale data center hub.

Mordor Intelligence projects that the Japanese data center market will expand from a value of US$ 11.89 billion in 2026 to US$ 17.66 billion by 2031. The country is experiencing a surge in hyperscale investment as AI model training pushes rack density higher. Commitments to expanding compute capacity are shortening supply-demand cycles, while also compressing permitting windows and intensifying competition for energy allocations, all adding tailwinds to Japan’s data center market expansion.

stories.content:
Singapore listed data center Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) plunged on November 17, just a day after the United States announced new export restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and computing infrastructure, raising concerns about the impact on operators serving customers across Southeast Asia. However, analysts say that the panic may be unwarranted.

According to a report by The Straits Times, on November 17, NTT DC REIT fell 0.5 percent, DigiCore REIT declined 2.2 percent and Keppel DC REIT lost nearly 1 percent. ST Engineering shares closed 1.9 percent lower at US$ 8.86, while Singtel rose 2.5 percent to US$ 4.10.

Meanwhile Reuters reported that Singapore’s Frencken, a supplier to Dutch chip equipment maker ASML, slid 3.91 percent, while semiconductor testing company AEM, which works with Intel, fell 2.9 percent.

But Mikhail Jaura, Head of Data Center Research for Asia Pacific, JLL told w.media, “The new US rule is primarily a compliance and licensing event rather than a demand shock. Operational capacity in Singapore is largely contracted on long-term leases, and the US-headquartered hyperscalers that anchor much of that demand are exempt from the new licence requirement, subject to reporting.”

He further explained, “The headwinds sit mainly in the forward pipeline, where projects reliant on non-US AI tenants now face licensing uncertainty, longer timelines and closer lender scrutiny. Rather than an erosion of confidence in AI infrastructure, we see a repricing of regulatory risk: demand for compute across Asia Pacific remains robust, and capital is likely to favour assets with transparent tenancy and strong compliance.”

Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist, Saxo Singapore too offered clarity on just who would feel the actual impact. “The biggest risks are for operators dependent on Chinese AI customers, where licensing uncertainty could affect utilisation, expansion plans and financing,” Chanana told The Straits Times. “Singapore remains an attractive regional data centre hub, but regulatory compliance and customer quality could increasingly determine which operators capture the next wave of AI investment.”

Therefore, the extent of the restrictions’ longer term impact will depend on operators’ exposure to affected customers, their ability to obtain export licenses, and whether their tenants qualify for exemptions.

Readers would recall that on Monday November 16, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced the Interim Final Rule (IFR) restricting chip exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Companies will now need licenses from the U.S. Commerce Department to ship advanced computing chips to these markets. The measure seeks to prevent sensitive U.S. chip technology from landing up in China’s hands, and also aims to prevent the restrictions from being circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.

Singapore’s government said it is reviewing the measure and engaging affected companies to assess its potential business impact. Although the announcement has raised concerns about licensing requirements and future expansion plans, analysts said the underlying demand for AI and cloud computing infrastructure remains intact.

stories.title: Trump-Xi-Putin talks: US-China relations, AI chips, Iran war among 5 things to watch
stories.summary: Leaders gather in Shenzhen for Apec Summit to discuss trade tensions and technology restrictions
stories.title_zh: 特朗普-习近平-普京会谈：中美关系、AI chips、伊朗战争等五大看点
stories.content:
Leaders gather in Shenzhen for Apec Summit to discuss trade tensions and technology restrictions

\[SINGAPORE\] US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are meeting on Thursday (Nov 19) in Shenzhen China for historic three-way talks.

Putin, Trump and Xi, as well as leaders from 21 Asia-Pacific economies arrived earlier for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, with high-stakes diplomacy and economic tensions threatening to overshadow the annual meeting.

The two-day meeting, which began on Wednesday, comes as the US and China navigate a fragile trade truce, Washington tightens restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports, and geopolitical disputes continue to test regional stability.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong will also be holding a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines.

Here are five things to watch at this year’s summit.

## 1. US-China relations

All eyes are on Trump and Xi as they meet in Shenzhen, with the trade truce between the world’s two largest economies due to expire in January 2027.

The two leaders last met in September in Washington, where they maintained a relatively conciliatory tone despite persistent disagreements over tariffs, technology restrictions and geopolitical issues.

Their latest meeting comes as both sides face pressure to prevent another escalation in trade tensions that could disrupt global markets and supply chains.

Xi has sought to portray China as a champion of economic openness. Speaking at the Apec CEO Summit on Wednesday, he pledged to cut tariffs, expand market access and improve conditions for foreign investors.

His remarks contrasted with Trump’s protectionist trade policies, which have raised concerns among economies dependent on international commerce.

Xi also called for closer technology partnerships and efforts to keep global supply chains stable and open.

The key question is whether the two leaders can extend their trade truce and prevent fresh disputes from undermining their relationship.

## 2. PM Wong’s agenda

For Singapore, the summit provides an opportunity to strengthen ties with regional partners as the Republic prepares to chair Asean in 2027.

Speaking at the Apec leaders’ meeting on Thursday, PM Wong urged economies to prevent the Asia-Pacific from splitting into “competing economic blocs”, warning that globalisation was becoming increasingly fragmented.

He called for progress towards an Asia-Pacific free trade area, stronger support for World Trade Organization reforms and a more flexible approach to multilateral cooperation, allowing willing economies to advance initiatives even without full consensus.

On Wednesday, PM Wong held bilateral meetings with Vietnamese President To Lam, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori.

The discussions covered trade, the digital economy, carbon credits and regional cooperation.

During his meeting with Lam, PM Wong highlighted opportunities for Singapore and Vietnam to support each other’s priorities next year, when Singapore chairs Asean and Vietnam chairs Apec.

He also discussed strengthening economic cooperation with Chile and Peru, including through existing trade agreements and new opportunities in the digital economy.

He said Singapore hoped to deepen collaboration with its partners amid growing global uncertainty.

PM Wong is scheduled to meet Xi on Friday, before travelling to Beijing for talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Saturday.

His engagements with China’s top leaders will be closely watched for indications of how Singapore intends to strengthen bilateral economic ties while navigating growing rivalry between major powers.

## 3. US-China chip, artificial intelligence race

The US-China technology rivalry has intensified ahead of the summit, following Washington’s announcement of tighter restrictions on advanced AI chips.

The new measures, announced on Monday, require export licences for certain advanced semiconductors shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil.

They also target overseas data centres that provide significant computing capacity to Chinese companies, as Washington seeks to prevent Beijing from circumventing existing export controls.

China has criticised the restrictions as economic coercion and warned that it would take necessary measures to protect its interests.

The move could complicate Trump-Xi talks, particularly as access to advanced chips remains central to both countries’ ambitions in AI.

The restrictions also have implications for Singapore, which is a major semiconductor trading hub and growing data centre market.

PM Wong said on Tuesday that Singapore could manage the impact on chips transhipped through the Republic, but was more concerned about those used by local companies and data centres.

Still, Singapore is pressing ahead with three national AI missions for financial services.

Whether Washington and Beijing can prevent their technology rivalry from escalating further will be a key development to watch.

Rare earths – crucial for the clean energy transition and electric vehicles – may also be discussed. The global supply is currently dominated by China and the US is struggling to catch up. On Tuesday, Trump gave a 10-month time frame, which analysts said is unlikely to happen.

## 4. Putin’s presence and geopolitics

Putin’s attendance marks his first in-person appearance at an Apec leaders’ meeting since 2017.

He is due to join Trump and Xi for a three-way meeting on Thursday, bringing together the leaders of three major nuclear powers.

Trump has previously floated denuclearisation as a possible discussion topic, although China has historically resisted negotiations over nuclear stockpile limits with Russia and the US, which possess much larger arsenals.

The meeting also takes place against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine and the conflict involving Iran.

A senior US administration official said Trump intended to discuss Iran with the two leaders but was not expected to raise Ukraine.

In his address to the Apec CEO Summit on Wednesday, Putin criticised Western sanctions and export restrictions, while highlighting Russia’s growing economic ties with the Asia-Pacific.

He said trade with the region now accounts for more than half of Russia’s total trade.

His presence gives Moscow an opportunity to deepen engagement with Asian economies despite Western efforts to isolate Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.

## 5. Regional disputes

Although Apec is primarily an economic forum, this year’s summit is taking place amid persistent security tensions in the Asia-Pacific.

Among the most contentious issues are competing territorial claims in the South China Sea, where China and several South-east Asian countries, including the Philippines and Vietnam, have overlapping claims.

The disputes have complicated efforts by Asean and China to conclude a Code of Conduct governing behaviour in the contested waters.

The Philippines ended its Asean chairmanship this week without securing a final agreement on the code, leaving the issue unresolved as Singapore prepares to take over the grouping’s leadership. The unfinished maritime negotiations remain among the key challenges facing the region.

Security concerns also extend to the Korean Peninsula, where North Korea’s nuclear weapons and missile programmes continue to unsettle neighbouring countries.

While such issues are not expected to dominate Apec’s formal economic discussions, they could feature in bilateral meetings and informal exchanges among leaders.

For Singapore, regional stability is closely linked to economic confidence and trade, making developments in the South China Sea and wider Asia-Pacific particularly significant.

Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Muhammad Sanusi Md Nor said the state is open to data centre investments, but the high consumption of land, water and electricity needs to be considered before approving any project.

“It is not that we do not want data centre investments, but at the KHTP, priority is given to industrial investments that can create more job opportunities for the people of the state.

“Among the areas that could be considered for data centres are Bakar Arang, Gurun, Bukit Kayu Hitam, Padang Terap and Padang Meha,” he said during his winding-up speech at the Kedah State Legislative Assembly sitting here on Wednesday.

Sanusi said a data centre typically creates only about 100 jobs, making its employment impact relatively smaller than that of factory and manufacturing investments.

Speaking to reporters at a press conference after the assembly sitting, he said two companies had submitted applications to develop data centres at the KHTP.

However, the state government had advised Kulim Technology Park Corporation (KTPC), which manages the technology park, to identify alternative locations.

“Site selection must take into account the capacity and availability of utilities, electricity, water and land to ensure that development does not affect the needs of other sectors,” he said.

stories.title: Alibaba's AI ambitions face steep challenge in US chip controls
stories.summary: Its results are due later on Thursday
stories.title_zh: 阿里巴巴的AI雄心面临美国chip controls的严峻挑战
stories.content:
Its results are due later on Thursday

ALIBABA Group Holding is facing mounting pressure to show it can deliver on its artificial intelligence business plan despite new limits on its access to data centre chips.

Its Hong Kong-listed shares capped a nine-day losing streak ahead of results due later on Thursday (Nov 19) from the internet firm. Alibaba’s market value stands at US$216 billion, less than half its level just over a year ago when investors were betting on it to lead the China’s AI industry.

Draft US rules announced on Monday would close a key workaround for Chinese hyperscalers to use advanced chips. That’s making analysts turn more cautious on Chinese AI companies’ cloud growth potential as well as their ability to train and run next-generation models.

“For Alibaba, they depend heavily on access to computing power, so this will be an important setback,” said Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak.

“It’s likely going to create a situation where it will take longer for them to build an ecosystem that can compete with the most advanced American technology.”

The new US rules are aimed at preventing Chinese firms from renting cutting-edge chips at data centres abroad.

Alibaba and its peers are already banned from direct buying the most advanced processors, and Nvidia said this week it is no longer shipping lower-end Hopper data centre chips to China as well.

Part of Alibaba’s ambition to build 20 gigawatts of data centre capacity before 2032 depends on expansion across regions like South-east Asia. Chips made in house by its T-Head unit may provide some buffer, but still trail the performance of Nvidia’s top products.

Fresh challenges aside, Alibaba’s results are expected to show a continued drag on its e-commerce business from sluggish Chinese consumption and tough competition.

Focus will be on whether that can be offset by its fast-growing cloud operation, which accounted for 18 per cent of total revenue in the June quarter.

Among its peers, Tencent Holdings posted results after Wednesday’s close showing a negative profit impact from heavy AI spending. The company also warned that Washington curbs on Chinese access to overseas data centres will hamper development of its next AI model.

Nevertheless, JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysts including Alex Yao expect US regulations to hurt Alibaba less than firms more directly exposed like MiniMax Group.

“The rule covers China-headquartered cloud providers operating abroad, but we estimate AliCloud’s overseas AI revenue at below 10 per cent of its cloud revenue, so the direct revenue impact is small,” they wrote in a note, maintaining overweight on Alibaba.

The bullish case is also bolstered by valuations, with the stock trading at about 10 times to forward earnings estimates. That’s down from its three-year average of nearly 13 times and similar to current multiples for Tencent and Baidu.

Nomura Holdings analysts including Jialong Shi are cautious on the impact of the new regulations overall, though they see leading hyperscalers holding up better.

“Independent AI labs, perhaps with the exception of DeepSeek, could face greater challenges in securing advanced Nvidia GPU capacity to train their next-generation models,” they wrote in a note on Tuesday. “Comparatively, Alibaba and ByteDance might be better positioned, in our view supported by their existing GPU resources and greater financial capabilities.” BLOOMBERG

stories.content:
Traders say Jensen Huang’s departure could potentially curb the chipmaker’s borrowing

NVIDIA’s credit-rating outlook was lowered to stable from positive by Moody’s Ratings, which cited governance concerns following the ouster of longtime chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

The move means that Nvidia’s Aa1 credit grade, the second-highest investment-grade rating, is unlikely to get a boost over the next 12 to 18 months, Moody’s said in a statement.

Huang’s exit “has introduced uncertainty about the company’s business strategy and financial policies,” analyst Raj Joshi wrote, noting that Nvidia’s market leadership and financial position remain “exceptionally strong.”

The world’s largest chipmaker cut ties with Huang on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman the US government has investigated for spying for China.

Huang’s departure could also weigh on Nvidia’s growth strategy, Joshi wrote, which is supported by the company’s “network of relationships across the AI ecosystem.” Government investigations into the events leading up to the exit could also “distract management,” he said.

The cost of protecting Nvidia’s debt against default has been declining since Huang’s departure. Its five-year credit default swaps were quoted at 121 basis points late Wednesday, about 20 basis points lower than a week ago.

Traders have said Huang’s departure could potentially curb the chipmaker’s borrowing, easing concerns about its credit profile.

Nvidia is at the centre of the artificial-intelligence ecosystem, having provided multibillion-dollar investments and financial backstops for AI infrastructure providers and model developers.

On Tuesday, however, Colette Kress, who’s been appointed as interim CEO, said the company will have a “disciplined” and “rigorous” approach to future investments across the AI supply chain. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: AMD buys World Labs & Taalas to boost AI strategy
stories.summary: The moves broaden AMD's reach from chips into AI model research and inference design as rivals race to control more of the technology stack.
stories.title_zh: AMD 收购 World Labs 与 Taalas 以增强 AI 战略
stories.content:
Thu, 19th Nov 2026 (Today)
AMD has completed its acquisitions of World Labs and Taalas, adding AI model research and inference chip design to its operations.

The deals expand AMD's reach across AI hardware, software and model development at a time when chipmakers are trying to secure more of the technology stack behind training and inference.

World Labs brings a research team focused on AI models that create and simulate interactive 3D environments, as well as robotic learning and simulation. The team will work with AMD engineers on future hardware, software and systems for the open AI ecosystem.

As part of the transaction, Dr Fei-Fei Li has joined AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to Chair and Chief Executive Officer Dr Lisa Su. Her arrival gives AMD a high-profile AI researcher as it seeks to link model design more closely with its chip and systems roadmap.

"Delivering the infrastructure that will power the next era of superintelligence requires us to optimize compute platforms and models together," said Dr Lisa Su, Chair and Chief Executive Officer of AMD. "We are thrilled to welcome Fei-Fei Li and the exceptional World Labs team to AMD. Their pioneering model research will help shape our future hardware, software and systems. Together, we will enable researchers and developers across the ecosystem to push the boundaries of what AI can do."

### Inference focus

Taalas adds a different part of the AI market. The company has been developing specialised silicon for AI inference, the stage at which trained models are deployed to answer queries or run applications.

The acquisition strengthens AMD's long-term inference roadmap. It plans to integrate Taalas technology into its accelerator strategy and build system-level products alongside Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs, ROCm software and its Helios rackscale offering.

The focus on inference reflects a wider market shift. While training large models remains a major spending category, chipmakers and cloud providers are also looking for ways to reduce the cost and power demands of serving AI models at scale, particularly as workloads become more specialised.

"AI inference is evolving rapidly, and customers need a broad range of compute solutions optimized for their workloads," said Vamsi Boppana, Senior Vice President of the Artificial Intelligence Group at AMD. "With Taalas now part of AMD, we're expanding our ability to deliver differentiated inference performance and efficiency, while strengthening our full-stack AI platform."

### Stack expansion

Taken together, the two acquisitions show AMD pursuing a broader AI strategy that extends beyond selling processors and accelerators. One brings frontier model expertise closer to the design of future computing systems, while the other adds technology aimed at AI deployment.

The approach mirrors an industry trend in which semiconductor groups are tightening links between silicon, systems software and AI model behaviour. For AMD, which has been building out its AI line-up around EPYC server processors and Instinct accelerators, the transactions also suggest a push to compete more directly across a wider range of workloads.

The World Labs team will continue foundational model research while collaborating with AMD engineers. In practice, AMD intends to use insights from emerging model behaviour to inform the design of future infrastructure.

The Taalas deal also expands AMD's engineering presence in Canada, giving it additional technical staff in a market where semiconductor and AI talent remain in high demand.

The acquisitions come as competition in AI infrastructure intensifies across training clusters, inference platforms and supporting software. Chip companies have increasingly turned to acquisitions to secure scarce expertise in model architecture, systems engineering and specialised silicon design.

AMD has not outlined financial terms in material released alongside the announcements, but it has made clear that both teams are intended to contribute directly to its AI product direction. World Labs adds research expertise at the model layer, while Taalas adds design work aimed at AI inference silicon and system integration.

The result is a broader internal AI bench spanning chips, software, systems and advanced model research, with Dr Fei-Fei Li joining AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, and the Taalas team extending the company's engineering base in Canada.

stories.title: Schneider Electric backs liquid cooling software for AI
stories.summary: The software could help AI data centres cut energy and water use while keeping hotter, denser GPU racks within safe operating limits.
stories.title_zh: Schneider Electric 支持面向 AI 的 liquid cooling 软件
stories.content:
Thu, 19th Nov 2026 (Today)
For AI factories, liquid cooling has become a thermodynamic necessity rather than a design choice. As rack power densities continue to rise, the challenge is no longer whether to deploy liquid cooling, but how to orchestrate cooling infrastructure at scale to optimize cost, efficiency, resilience, and GPU utilization.

Liquid cooling orchestration offers the ability to manage cooling as a system rather than as a collection of individual assets, which helps ensure that cooling capacity efficiently matches AI workloads at any given time, while minimizing waste. In doing so, it can deliver cost savings by improving power usage effectiveness (PUE) and water usage effectiveness (WUE). What's more, orchestration software can help optimize data center design and construction costs by giving owners more accurate data on how much power and water they'll need for cooling in the facility in any specific location.

Liquid cooling orchestration transforms cooling from a collection of interdependent systems managed through separate local controls into a coordinated thermal management platform for the AI factory. By maintaining the required heat rejection and thermal headroom as workload conditions change, operators can maximize GPU performance, improve cooling-capacity utilization, and reduce unnecessary energy or water use.

Orchestration enables operational intelligence, which improves power usage effectiveness (PUE) and water usage effectiveness (WUE) and drives real-time analytics and diagnostics across cooling, power, and workload conditions. It also enables autonomous optimization of thermal performance, energy efficiency, water consumption, and capacity utilization.

The result is a more resilient, sustainable, and economically optimized AI factory capable of supporting today's workloads as well as next-generation GPU deployments at scale.

**What is liquid cooling orchestration and what are its benefits?**

AI factories typically use a hybrid thermal architecture that combines liquid-to-chip cooling infrastructure for high-density AI workloads with air-cooling systems for building and other IT equipment. The cooling ecosystem may include coolant distribution units (CDUs), pumping systems, liquid distribution networks, CRAHs (computer room air handlers), fan walls, chillers, dry coolers, cooling towers, and adiabatic heat rejection technologies.

AI workloads can fluctuate rapidly, but the thermal, hydraulic, and mechanical systems that support liquid cooling operate on much slower timescales. As a result, liquid cooling orchestration aims not to react to individual GPU load changes, but to continuously optimize the end-to-end cooling ecosystem so sufficient cooling capacity is available when needed while minimizing energy, water, and infrastructure overhead.

The idea is to maintain thermal headroom and optimize supervisory setpoints over seconds-to-minutes and minutes-to-hours, depending on the equipment involved. Fluid volume, metal mass, and allowable temperature rise provide a temporary thermal buffer while slower equipment responds.

Orchestration software also continuously learns from historical and real-time data, then coordinates chillers, heat rejection equipment, CDUs, pumps, and airflow systems to achieve system-wide outcomes. Predictive analytics can help anticipate sustained thermal demand, identify abnormal conditions, and recommend supervisory adjustments to maximize overall facility efficiency.

**How do I manage mixed air and liquid environments?**

Cooling orchestration software ingests real-time telemetry and operational data from both liquid and air-cooling infrastructure. It provides a unified operational view of the thermal infrastructure, enabling coordinated control and optimization across both air and liquid cooling domains. This is crucial because AI environments often consist of multiple server platforms with different thermal profiles and cooling architectures.

**How do I optimize cooling across multiple sites?**

As AI factories expand across regions and geographies, cooling optimization increasingly becomes a fleet management consideration. Cooling orchestration software provides a centralized view of thermal performance, infrastructure utilization, energy efficiency, and water consumption across sites, enabling operators and stakeholders to benchmark these AI data centers, identify underperforming assets, and standardize best practices. By applying lessons learned from high performing data centers across the broader fleet, operators can improve operational consistency, maximize cooling infrastructure utilization, and reduce the total cost of operating large scale AI deployments.

**How do I coordinate thermal and compute workloads?**

Cooling orchestration software uses AI to add intelligence around cooling capacity decisions. For NVIDIA GPUs, for example, the software considers MAX-LPS, MAX-P, and MAX-Q Profile configurations to meet the desired performance requirements with "just right" cooling capacity.

Intelligent software continuously monitors real-time GPU and rack power telemetry as a leading indicator of heat load, correlated with manifold return temperature and flow. Using predictive AI models, it anticipates workload driven thermal demand and proactively recommends or automatically adjusts CDU and chilled water plant setpoints, so cooling capacity is in place before heat reaches the coolant loop.

**How can liquid cooling orchestration improve data center efficiency?**

As liquid cooling becomes more prevalent in AI data centers, hyperscalers, colocation providers, neoclouds, and other data center operators have an opportunity to improve efficiency by managing cooling as a coordinated system rather than as individual components.

Local CDU control loops hold supply temperature and differential pressure within expected operational ranges, while orchestration operates at the supervisory layer. Fully automated, or operator approved, orchestration can continuously reset setpoints across the heat rejection plant, chillers, CDUs, and secondary fluid network to keep adequate thermal headroom at the cold plate with the least energy and water use. Managing the full heat transfer chain as one system, from the cold plate to heat rejection, lets operators run warmer supply temperatures, gain more economizer hours, cut pumping energy, and recover stranded cooling capacity without compromising thermal resilience or GPU performance.

Liquid cooling orchestration can also extend beyond day-to-day operations. By providing greater visibility into actual cooling requirements and performance across sites, cooling orchestration software can help operators optimize capacity, identify best practices, and make more informed infrastructure investments. This can help avoid unnecessary capital expenditures, reduce operating costs, and support more efficient, scalable AI infrastructure.

stories.why_zh: 尽管面临企业层面逆风，Tencent的cloud增长表明Chinese AI需求足以抵消更广泛的技术行业疲软，但随着国际扩张面临地缘政治障碍，公司对国内基础设施的依赖变得更加明显。结果表明，为Chinese企业服务的cloud和data center运营商可以预期需求持续保持韧性，即使面向消费者的数字服务遭遇监管摩擦。
stories.content:
Its topline rises 8% for the quarter to 207.3 billion yuan, below an LSEG consensus estimate

\[BEIJING\] China’s Tencent reported an 8 per cent climb in third-quarter revenue on Wednesday (Nov 18), weaker than both expectations and results for the previous quarter as growth for its gaming businesses cooled.

But demand for artificial intelligence services lifted its cloud business, a key focus for investors who are monitoring whether Tencent’s heavy AI spending is starting to pay off or if it is mainly squeezing margins.

The tech giant reported revenue of 207.3 billion yuan (US$31.1 billion) for the three months ended September, a little below an LSEG consensus estimate of 210.8 billion yuan. It booked 11 per cent growth in the previous quarter.

Revenue from fintech and business services, which includes the cloud unit, rose 9 per cent to 63.7 billion yuan, with demand for AI-related cloud services a key driver.

“Our cloud services revenue growth rate increased, driven by WorkBuddy, and as we allocated more compute to Model as a Service and GPU rental,” Tencent chief executive officer Pony Ma said, referring to the company’s cloud business.

Compared to US companies, Chinese tech giants have been somewhat on the back foot, as they have struggled to obtain advanced Nvidia chips because of US export restrictions.

Tencent said a year ago that chip shortages were constraining its cloud growth, as it prioritised using AI chips internally over renting computing power to external clients.

Washington this week announced new rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips through overseas data centres. Following the news, shares in Chinese cloud service providers, including Tencent, slid on Tuesday.

Revenue from value-added services, which include Tencent’s gaming business, rose just 3 per cent to 98.3 billion yuan in the third quarter. Domestic games revenue grew 11 per cent, while international games revenue slid 9 per cent.

Net profit edged up 0.8 per cent to 63.61 billion yuan, beating analyst expectations of 59.46 billion yuan.

Capital expenditure in the September quarter was 81.4 billion yuan, compared with 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter. Tencent spent 84.7 billion yuan in the first half of the year, more than the roughly 79 billion yuan it spent in all of 2025. REUTERS

stories.content:
(Nov 18): Tencent Holdings Ltd conceded that new Washington curbs on Chinese access to overseas data centres will hamper development of its next artificial intelligence (AI) model, though the country will move increasingly towards domestic semiconductors to mitigate the longer-term impact.

“It sets everyone back in China,” Tencent president Martin Lau told analysts on a post-earnings call on Wednesday. “It would take probably a longer time for us to come up with the next version in the short run.”

The US Department of Commerce on Monday introduced a rule that curbs Chinese companies’ remote access to cutting-edge Nvidia Corp silicon in data centres abroad, plugging a longtime loophole that helped the likes of Tencent and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. The regulation also makes it harder for AI chips to be smuggled into China via Southeast Asia because of new US licensing requirements.

The directive will help accelerate the development of the domestic chip supply chain in China, Lau said. That should allow Chinese companies to reduce a heavy reliance on Nvidia processors, considered the gold standard for the industry.

Huawei Technologies Co has spearheaded the country’s efforts to come up with alternatives, though its technology still lags behind global leaders.

“All Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips,” Lau said. “All the development effort would actually have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.”

stories.summary: ByteDance faces dual setbacks in Malaysia as financing for a data center project developed with Epoch has been delayed and a loan intended for Nvidia chip purchases has been frozen. The complications arise amid intensifying US scrutiny of Chinese technology investments in Southeast Asian digital infrastructure.

stories.title_zh: ByteDance 马来西亚 data center 计划在两线受阻
stories.summary_zh: ByteDance在Malaysia遭遇双重挫折，其与Epoch合作开发的data center项目融资被推迟，用于购买Nvidia芯片的贷款也被冻结。这些复杂情况出现在美国加强对Chinese企业在Southeast Asian数字基础设施投资的审查之际。
stories.why_zh: 随着金融和监管渠道同时收紧，Chinese hyperscale企业获取海外AI能力的空间正在缩小，迫使ByteDance及同行加速国内基础设施建设或接受性能劣势。对Malaysia而言，这一停滞的投资考验着其在管理大国技术竞争的同时成为中立区域枢纽的雄心。
stories.content:
TikTok owner ByteDance has hit two snags in Malaysia, with financing for a data center it plans to use delayed and a loan to fund the purchase of Nvidia chips frozen.

Looking at the data center project, Bloomberg reports that a presentation scheduled for earlier this month, in which data center developer and operator Epoch Digital would pitch a US$ 488 million loan to banks, was delayed. A planned visit to the site also didn’t happen.

While it was reported that HSBC Holdings Plc, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp., and Bank of China have signed the loan and committed to providing Epoch with the capital, the missed presentation will postpone the syndication process. The presentation and site visit are important for due diligence lenders must undertake before deciding to participate in syndication.

According to a person familiar with the matter, Epoch Digital’s management wasn’t available on November 2, 2026, for the presentation or the site visit that same week, prompting the delay.

In a separate matter, a US$ 480 million loan meant to fund the purchase of AI chips for a Malaysian data center being developed by Aolani Cloud Pte, a Singapore-based neocloud serving ByteDance, has been frozen. The freeze came after the US revealed new rules for exports of advanced semiconductor technology to Singapore, Malaysia, and several other countries.

“We have spent significant time with our banking and financing partners to assess and anticipate regulatory risk ahead of this recent new ruling,” a spokesperson for Aolani told Bloomberg. “We are pro-actively working with regulators and our financing partners to ensure the project delivery goes ahead in full compliance with the new ruling.”

According to its sources, the publication says that the funding won’t progress until the bankers can fully evaluate the new rules coming out of the US. Some bankers have reportedly said the facility is dead in the water given the risk it carries if it violates the new rule.

In October, Aolani announced it had signed letters of intent to take up 500 MW of AI data center capacity in Malaysia, bringing its total capacity commitment in the country to 580 MW, with around 80 MW already earmarked for 2026. It’s unclear at this stage whether those commitments will face similar delays as a result of the new US rule.

The US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce are currently investigating Singapore-based cloud computing and AI infrastructure provider Megaspeed on suspicions that its Malaysian operations are involved in potential semiconductor diversion and re-exports of Nvidia chips. As w.media reported ,Megaspeed has said that it has cooperated with inspections conducted by the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security and will cooperate with any other relevant authority in future.

stories.title: China seeks advanced Nvidia chips for AI weapons despite US curbs
stories.summary: China's military is seeking advanced Nvidia chips for AI-enabled weapons as Chinese-made processors continue to lag US rivals, a congressional commission said in its annual report released on Wednesday.

stories.content:
(Nov 18): China's military is seeking advanced Nvidia chips for AI-enabled weapons as Chinese-made processors continue to lag US rivals, a congressional commission said in its annual report released on Wednesday.

The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission said Beijing was seeking to circumvent US export controls to obtain advanced semiconductors critical to its push for "intelligentised warfare," the People's Liberation Army's term for integrating artificial intelligence into weapons, command and control, kill chains and logistics.

"China is seeking to evade US export controls to gain the most advanced semiconductors that underpin its intelligentisation drive," according to the report.

Domestic AI chips, including Huawei's Ascend and Cambricon's Siyuan series, still trail more advanced products from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, according to the report.

The findings add to scrutiny of Nvidia's China business following the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang over his extramarital affairs, including one with a former executive of a Singapore-based business partner whom US authorities suspected of spying for China.

Earlier this week, *Reuters* reported that Chinese entities were adopting increasingly sophisticated methods to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals.

Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China's AI data-centre market, though a *Reuters* review found more than US$3 billion (RM12.4 billion) in Chinese computing projects using its restricted chips.

Washington said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to advanced chips from companies including Nvidia.

Separately, the Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, an effort to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or Beijing, *Reuters* reported exclusively on Wednesday.

stories.title: Orange seeks partners to extend ReuNION subsea cable to Singapore
stories.summary: Orange hopes to extend a new subsea cable linking the French-African island of La Réunion to South Africa further to Southeast Asia and make La Réunion a major landing hub.
stories.title_zh: Orange寻求合作伙伴将ReuNION海底电缆延伸至Singapore
stories.content:
Orange hopes to extend a new subsea cable linking the French-African island of La Réunion to South Africa further to Southeast Asia and make La Réunion a major landing hub.

The French telco and consortium members La Réunion Connectée and Reunicable et Telco Oi this week announced hopes to extend ReuNION and “position La Réunion as an interconnection point between Europe, Africa and Asia.”

First announced in September, the first phase of ReuNION will link La Réunion to South Africa. Marine studies are underway, and cable deployment is scheduled for 2027 and 2028, with provisional launch expected in early 2029.

The consortium is now seeking investors and partners for a second phase that would extend the system to Singapore.

The La Réunion to South Africa section carries 16 fiber pairs, each offering 20 Tbps for a total capacity of 320 Tbps. The Singapore extension would scale to 24 fiber pairs.

Phase 1 is supported by European funding through the Connecting Europe Facility and the European Regional Development Fund.

Orange said the system’s open-cable design means future co-investors can add branching units and choose landing points, including Mauritius, Madagascar and Mayotte, as well as India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Maldives.

Réunicable SAS, founded in April 2011, is a telecoms provider in Réunion, operating an island-wide fiber network. La Réunion Connectée is the island’s digital-focused public institution.

Réunion is an island in the Indian Ocean, and an overseas department and region of France. It is located approximately 679 kilometres (367 nautical miles) east of the island of Madagascar and 175 kilometres (94 nmi) southwest of the island of Mauritius.

There are currently three subsea cables landing in Réunion in Saint Paul, Le Port, and Sainte Marie.

The first subsea cable to land in Réunion was the SAFE cable, a consortium system dating back to 2002 and linking South Africa to India and Malaysia. This was followed by the Orange-led LION system in 2009 linking the island to Madagascar and Mauritius, and then in 2021 with the METISS system linking the three African islands to South Africa.

The SAFE cable is scheduled for decommissioning in 2027, leaving METISS as the island’s only international cable.

Orange, one of the major telecoms providers in Réunion, is currently in the process of shutting off its copper network on the island. The shutoff started last year in January 2025 and is due to be completed in 2030.

Globally, Orange is involved in more than 40 submarine cables, totaling nearly 450,000 km (279,617 miles) of fiber. In May, the firm announced plans for a pan-African subsea cable system named Via Africa. The system is set to run from the UK down to Cape Horn.

stories.title: Next Capital launches new Australian data center firm Dataspace
stories.summary: Australian investment firm Next Capital has established Dataspace, a new data center platform targeting the mid-market enterprise and government segments with facilities in Sydney and Melbourne. The venture represents private equity's continued appetite for Australian digital infrastructure despite rising development costs and power constraints.
stories.why_it_matters: Dataspace's entry intensifies competition for the underserved mid-market segment between hyperscale-focused incumbents, potentially improving service diversity and pricing for enterprises unable to secure space in premium facilities. However, the platform's success depends on navigating Australia's increasingly constrained transmission infrastructure, where queue delays for grid connection now routinely extend 24-36 months.
stories.title_zh: Next Capital成立新澳大利亚数据中心公司Dataspace
stories.summary_zh: Australian投资公司Next Capital成立了Dataspace，这是一个新的data center平台，瞄准Sydney和Melbourne的中端企业市场和政府细分市场。该投资表明，尽管开发成本和电力限制上升，private equity对Australian数字基础设施的兴趣仍在持续。

stories.content:
Australian private equity firm Next Capital has launched a new data center operator, seeded with several facilities acquired from Fujitsu earlier this year.

Next Capital acquired the Japanese company's data center business in Australia in July via its AU$375 million (US$262.76m) fifth fund, taking over operations at five data centers across Australia.

This week saw the launch of Dataspace, a new data center operator owned by Next Capital, operating from the acquired facilities.

Dataspace operates five data centers around Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth.

According to local press, Fujitsu Asia Pacific head of transformation service delivery Gavin Milton-White has been appointed as Dataspace’s CEO.

“We are starting with a very strong platform including established facilities, experienced people, long-standing customers and infrastructure that has been operating reliably for decades,” Milton-White told ARN. “Our job is to build on these strengths. We have capacity we can offer customers today, further space within the existing facilities that we can bring online quickly as demand grows and, over time, the ability to develop substantially more capacity on our existing sites.”

The company has sites in Homebush and Greystanes, New South Wales (2.8MW across 1,885 sqm and 7MW across 9,000 sqm, respectively); Eight Mile Plains, Queensland (1MW across 750 sqm); Noble Park, Victoria (2MW across 3,050 sqm); and Malaga, Western Australia (1.7MW across 3,125 sqm).

Founded in 2005, Next Capital is a mid-market private equity firm. The company has some data center history, acquiring Australian data center firm iseek in 2018 and selling it to Amber Infrastructure in 2021. Fujitsu had reportedly been seeking a buyer for its Aussie data center assets since 2024.

Next Capital partner James Murphy told ARN: “What attracted us to this business was the quality of the underlying platform, including the facilities, the customer base, the operating track record and, importantly, the people. We see a significant opportunity to support Dataspace with further investment as it enters its next stage of growth.”

Dataspace should not be confused with Russian data center firm DataSpace, which was founded in 2009 and operates a colocation facility in Moscow.

stories.title: AMD and PsiQuantum to co-design infrastructure to support hybrid classical-quantum compute
stories.summary: AMD has partnered with PsiQuantum to co-design compute infrastructure that will support utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers and hybrid classical-quantum applications.
stories.title_zh: AMD与PsiQuantum将联合设计支持混合经典-量子计算的基础设施
stories.content:
AMD has partnered with PsiQuantum to co-design compute infrastructure that will support utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers and hybrid classical-quantum applications.

Under the terms of the agreement, AMD said it plans to make an equity investment in PsiQuantum, but did not disclose the size of the proposed stake.

The collaboration will expand the partners’ current work around AMD’s Versal FPGA (field-programmable gate array) offering, which PsiQuantum previously selected for its quantum computing platform, to include AMD’s broader GPU, CPU, and ROCm software technology stack, alongside PsiQuantum’s silicon photonics offering.

FPGA chips consist of logic blocks that can be configured by the customer on the spot to accelerate specific workloads. These programmable chips can then sit alongside microprocessors to make hardware that is faster and more open to a software-defined approach.

The partnership aligns with the US Department of Energy’s Quantum Genesis Priority Applications, which is aiming to identify a key set of scientific problems that fault-tolerant quantum computers will be expected to solve, the companies said in a statement.

“Quantum computing will enable solving problems in healthcare, materials, energy, finance, and other domains that are out of reach today, working in concert with AI and high-performance computing,” said Victor Peng, CEO of PsiQuantum. “By bringing our teams and technologies together, PsiQuantum and AMD will advance the future of computing, from the infrastructure that supports utility-scale quantum systems to new approaches for networking with silicon photonics and scaling the foundations of next-gen AI.”

Mark Papermaster, EVP, CTO, AMD, added: “AMD has a long track record of bringing together the compute technologies and deep engineering partnerships needed to build the world’s most powerful supercomputers and AI infrastructure. We see that same opportunity with quantum computing, where leadership in classical computing is essential to building systems at scale. Our work with PsiQuantum brings the breadth of AMD compute and software to this next frontier, combining our strengths to accelerate the path to utility-scale quantum computing.”

stories.title: Stop giving data centres cheaper coal-based electricity to protect households, says Yeo Bee Yin

The proposal would increase data center power costs while accelerating renewable energy procurement.

If adopted, the policy would compress data center developer margins in Malaysia while creating a template for other Southeast Asian nations to renegotiate the terms of their digital infrastructure attraction strategies, potentially redirecting investment toward markets with more advanced renewable frameworks.

stories.summary_zh: 前Malaysian能源部长Yeo Bee Yin呼吁将燃煤发电从用于为data center定价电力的基础电价计算中剔除，她认为为工业用户提供补贴的化石电力最终会加重家庭消费者负担。该提议将增加data center电力成本，同时加速可再生能源采购。

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): Former energy minister Yeo Bee Yin on Wednesday urged the government to exclude coal-fired generations from the calculation of base tariff for data centres to protect households in the longer term.

The Puchong MP argued that households should retain the benefit of cheaper electricity while large new users face prices that better reflect their supply costs.

She called on the Energy Commission (EC) to review and implement this exclusion immediately, rather than wait until a separate wholesale electricity market for large consumers is introduced years from now.

“We should price electricity for data centres correctly even now. Not \[wait\] until 2029 and 2030,” she told the Dewan Rakyat during the committee-stage debate on electricity supply allocation on Wednesday.

Yeo argued that excluding the coal component from data-centre tariff calculations would help keep household electricity costs under control, while allowing targeted investors to assess whether their business models remained viable.

Building any new power plants to meet uncertain demand could ultimately leave other consumers bearing the costs if market conditions or technology changed and the anticipated demand failed to materialise, she warned.

“Data centres can be built within 12 to 24 months — that's one to two years. Meanwhile, gas-fired power plants will now take four to seven years, taking into account supply chain constraints,” Yeo said.

To ease pressure before new generation capacity becomes available, she urged the government to strengthen measures that encourage large users, including factories, to reduce peak electricity demand.

She also proposed extending tax incentives to companies leasing battery energy storage systems, which will allow factories to install storage without substantial upfront expenditure.

Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof, who is also the energy transition and water transformation minister, had in mid-October hinted that a “user-pays” pricing approach was being considered to shield households from rising electricity costs. However, details on rates, consumption thresholds and implementation timelines have yet to be announced.

His deputy, Datuk Seri Abdul Rahman Mohamad, shared on Wednesday that Peninsular Malaysia’s electricity reserve margin was projected at 24%-27% for 2027-2035. According to the EC, the country's reserve margin stood at 25% in 2025.

For now, the government had increased connected load charges to discourage excessive capacity bookings by data centres and introduced an ultra-high-voltage tariff structure effective July 1, 2025, he added.

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 18): Northern Solar Holdings Bhd (KL:NORTHERN) plans to raise as much as RM42.99 million via a private placement of up to 10% of its issued shares to partially fund its solar projects for two data centres in Johor.

The placement will see up to 39.56 million new shares issued to third-party investors, according to the group’s bourse filing on Wednesday.

The identity of the investors and the issue price of the placement shares will be decided later, Northern Star said.

The group said the estimated RM42.99 million proceeds are based on an illustrative issue price of RM1.0868 per share, which is based on Northern Solar’s five-day volume-weighted average market price up to Oct 26.

Earlier this month, Northern Solar's wholly-owned subsidiary, Northern Solar Assets Sdn Bhd, was awarded two solar projects under the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS).

The projects have a combined capacity of 189 megawatts coupled with battery storage systems and carry a combined estimated cost of RM840 million.

Northern Star plans to allocate RM21.45 million each for the two projects from the proceeds of the private placement.

The group did not say how it plans to fund the remaining cost of the projects.

If the deal is exercised, Northern Solar expects its gearing ratio to drop to 0.08 times from 0.12 times, while its net assets per share will improve to 29 sen from 21 sen.

At the same time, the shareholdings of substantial shareholders — managing director Lew Shoong Kai and executive director Chew Win Hoe — will each be diluted to 21.61% from 23.77%.

The placement is expected to be completed by the fourth quarter of 2026, the group said.

UOB Kay Hian (M) Sdn Bhd and Alliance Islamic Bank Bhd are the other joint placement agents for the private placement.

Northern Solar transferred its listing from Bursa Malaysia's ACE Market to the Main Market on Oct 6.

The group is principally involved in providing engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) services for solar photovoltaic projects, renewable energy generation, and the operations and maintenance of solar systems.

As of October, the group said its unbilled order book stood at RM2.90 billion with a tender book of RM2.1 billion that includes submissions for utilities and large scale solar projects.

Northern Solar shares closed two sen or 2.3% higher at 89 sen on Wednesday, valuing the group at RM352.1 million. The counter has risen over 30% over the past one year.

stories.summary: Woolpert, a global architecture, engineering, and geospatial consulting firm, has acquired B-Global Tech, a Barcelona-based architecture and engineering firm that specializes in the design and delivery of digital infrastructure projects in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia-Pacific. Through the acquisition, Woolpert will strengthen its ability to support data centers and other mission-critical facilities across […]
stories.title_zh: Woolpert 收购 B-Global Tech 以扩展全球数据中心业务
stories.content:
Woolpert, a global architecture, engineering, and geospatial consulting firm, has acquired B-Global Tech, a Barcelona-based architecture and engineering firm that specializes in the design and delivery of digital infrastructure projects in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia-Pacific. Through the acquisition, Woolpert will strengthen its ability to support data centers and other mission-critical facilities across the globe.

The acquisition also increases Woolpert’s pool of professionals focused on the responsible design of data center infrastructure to more than 1,200, it said in a press release. The technical depth B-Global Tech brings to the table means Woolpert will be able to improve its ability to deliver data center programs.

“B-Global Tech brings exceptional data center expertise and an established presence in some of the world’s most important digital infrastructure markets,” said Neil Churman, Woolpert President and Chief Executive Officer. “Together, we are building a truly global mission critical practice with the specialized expertise, multidisciplinary capabilities, and scale to help our clients deliver increasingly complex infrastructure with greater certainty while ensuring these facilities are designed and developed responsibly and in line with local requirements.”

Woolpert has worked for data center operators including Equinix, NextDC, Digital Realty, and Vantage Data Centers, and has designed more than 8.8 million square meters of data center space. B-Global Tech has deep expertise in hyperscale, colocation, and AI facilities and has delivered projects ranging from supercomputing centers to data center campuses of up to 500 MW.

“This is an exciting opportunity to build on what our people have created at B-Global Tech while expanding the opportunities available to our teams and clients,” said Lluis Gironella Ferrer, B-Global Tech Co-founder. “Joining Woolpert connects our people to a global network of expertise and resources, creating new opportunities to collaborate across markets and giving clients a premier architecture and engineering design firm they can trust to support their AI data center needs worldwide.”

The data center construction market is projected to grow from a value of US$ 300.4 billion in 2026 to US$ 460.2 billion by 2032, according to Mordor Intelligence. Mordor Intelligence expects developers facing higher site costs and renewable-supply conditions on grid connections to favor contractors that coordinate design, electrical, and cooling work.

stories.title: Who watches over Nvidia's chips?
stories.summary: A scandal about Washington, not just one CEO
stories.title_zh: 谁在监管NVIDIA的chips？
stories.content:
A scandal about Washington, not just one CEO

FOR two years, the fight over selling artificial intelligence chips to China ran on abstractions: compute thresholds, “fourth-best” chips, market share versus military uplift. In the last three weeks it acquired a plot.

The events unfolded rapidly. Within 14 days of *The New York Times* reporting that US agencies had examined whether a businesswoman at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI cloud company and major Nvidia customer, was working for Chinese intelligence, Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang and resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago.

It is tempting to read this as a morality tale about one man. That misses the bigger story. The fight that matters is the one now in the open.

It involves Washington’s China hawks, Congress, US President Donald Trump’s own Cabinet and the Commerce Department under Howard Lutnick, which licenses chip exports and keeps the Entity List, the government’s trade blacklist.

## Commerce’s failings

The hawks’ case rests on a pattern that Commerce has not convincingly explained. Its export-enforcement arm has had Megaspeed in its sights since late 2024.

The US has imposed chip-export restrictions since 2022, but officials reportedly found Nvidia equipment still boxed at a Malaysian data centre; an affiliated company has since bought at least US$4.8 billion of Nvidia-based gear.

Other agencies have reportedly urged adding Megaspeed to the Entity List. But the company remains off the list, to which Commerce has, by several counts, added no one in more than 13 months.

Lutnick reportedly received a classified memo about Jensen Huang’s relationship before Trump’s May trip to Beijing, the same trip during which Commerce cleared about 10 Chinese companies to buy H200s. The exact date that the memo was sent, relative to those approvals, has not been reported.

What changes the shape of the fight is who is on the other side. According to Axios, Trump approved action against suspected chip diversion at least three times, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in support of the crackdown and Lutnick warning that it would spark a trade war.

Bessent reportedly asked Lutnick in the Situation Room why Megaspeed wasn’t listed, and Lutnick allegedly said he didn’t know. Commerce denies the exchange took place.

This is not Democrats against the administration, or Congress against the executive. It is conflict within the administration, with the treasury, state, defence departments and the trade office against Commerce.

## Commerce’s response

The US Commerce Department has a few defences for its actions.

First, Commerce’s chip policy was the president’s policy. In January, Trump chose to allow H200 sales to China in exchange for a 25 per cent cut of the revenue, and Lutnick has repeatedly said that, on Beijing, he follows the White House’s lead.

Second, the department says it enforces “by the book”, uses the Entity List against bad actors as a matter of routine and closed an AI-chip export loophole in May.

Third, part of the Megaspeed delay has a procedural explanation: Commerce reportedly paused its own probe at the Justice Department’s request, and listing a target in the middle of a criminal investigation can tip the company off.

Fourth, the espionage case is unproven. CNN reports that US intelligence is not certain Alice Huang actually spied on Nvidia. Megaspeed says it is a compliant, legal corporation.

Beijing calls the allegation groundless. Nvidia’s board states it had no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised.

Finally, the substantive case for selling, that American chips in Chinese data centres keep China dependent on the US technology stack and deny Huawei customers, is a serious position. It pre-dates this scandal, and the scandal does not refute it.

## Washington’s process failures

Here is the uncomfortable point for both camps.

As a former Commerce official told CNN, Beijing did not need an intelligence operation to get Nvidia lobbying for China sales.

Jensen Huang argued for them openly and once dismissed the label “China hawk” as a badge of shame. If Alice Huang was an asset, she was pushing on an open door. The spy angle alone does not show that US policy was corrupted.

But that cuts against Commerce, too. What the scandal exposes is not one compromised executive. It is an export-enforcement agency that appears to have let trade diplomacy override its enforcement tools.

The unheeded memo, the frozen Entity List, the stalled curbs and the unanswered question in the Situation Room – if the exchange did take place – are arguably process failures. They would matter even if Alice Huang turns out to be nothing more than a businesswoman.

Trump’s comment that the memo did not make much of an impact on his decision-making process does not help Commerce’s case.

A person can believe that selling H200s to vetted Chinese buyers is smart policy and also believe that a company under a years-long chip-diversion investigation belongs on the Entity List.

Those positions are compatible. The administration’s failure to keep them separate, treating every enforcement action as a chip to trade with Beijing, is the real lesson of the Nvidia affair.

The hawks now have what one analyst called a story with a name and a face. They should resist overclaiming: The espionage is unproven, and the argument for selling chips to China did not begin with Alice Huang.

But the case against Commerce does not depend on who she was.

It depends on whether America’s export-control system works when enforcing it is diplomatically inconvenient. On the record so far, it has not.
